name: Labdanum

lead: Labdanum is a dark, sticky resin collected from the leaves and stems of rockrose shrubs (Cistus ladanifer and Cistus creticus) around the Mediterranean. Perfumers use it as a core ingredient in amber and chypre scents, where it gives a warm, resinous, slightly leathery depth and helps a fragrance last.

For appearance, its main role is scent: it appears in colognes and perfumes that people wear as part of their grooming. Laboratory research has also looked at extracts for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and anti-elastase activity, which is why it is discussed as a possible skincare ingredient, but this work has been done in vitro rather than in human skin trials.

paras: People encounter labdanum through finished fragrances rather than on its own; perfume labels may list it as labdanum, cistus or ciste absolute. It is also used as a fixative, a material that helps a scent last longer. Cosmetic use in creams is mostly at the research or niche-product stage.

As with many natural fragrance materials, it can cause skin sensitization or irritation in some people, and the raw resin has a strong scent. Industry standards govern how much can be used in formulas. Skin-related benefits reported in laboratory studies have not been confirmed in people.

angle.text: Labdanum gives fragrances their warm amber base and helps them last on the skin, so wearing a scent built on it adds to a person's grooming. Its use as a skincare ingredient is at an earlier, laboratory stage.

lead: Labdanum (also ladanum or ladanon) is a dark, viscous resin exuded by rockrose shrubs of the genus Cistus, mainly Cistus ladanifer in the western Mediterranean and Cistus creticus in the east [1][2]. It has been gathered since antiquity for incense and traditional medicine and is now produced mainly for the perfume industry [3].

In perfumery it is a key ingredient in amber accords and chypre fragrances; its scent is described as rich, sweet, leathery and ambergris-like, and it is valued as a plant-derived alternative to ambergris [3][1]. For people interested in how they smell, it is one of the materials behind warm, resinous colognes.

Researchers have also studied labdanum and Cistus extracts for biological properties including antioxidant and antimicrobial activity, and note possible cosmetic, pharmaceutical and food applications [4]. A 2020 laboratory study found a purified labdanum fraction suppressed dengue virus in cell culture [5]. These findings come from lab work, not human trials.
infobox: Mediterranean: Iberia, southern France, North Africa, Crete

paras: The resin is produced on the leaves and stems of gum rockrose. C. ladanifer is an evergreen shrub of the western Mediterranean with sticky leaves [1][2]. The raw gum is dark and plastic, becomes brittle with age and is typically extracted by boiling; solvent extraction gives an absolute and steam distillation gives an essential oil [3].

Chemically, a review of the plant describes a characteristic exudate composition and proposes a plant-specific carotenoid derivative as a marker of authenticity for aromatic and pharmaceutical uses [1]. Essential-oil work lists alpha-pinene, viridiflorol and camphene among the main constituents [4].

Labdanum is produced mainly for perfumes and is a cornerstone of amber accords and chypre fragrances; its smell is described with words such as amber, sweet, powdery, leathery and animalic [3]. It has been used as a fixative and as a substitute for ambergris, which is restricted in many countries [3][2].
Wikipedia also notes older uses in incense and herbal medicine [3].

A 2025 review of C. ladanifer essential oils and by-products describes antioxidant and antimicrobial properties and says the plant could have uses in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and food [4]. A Grokipedia summary of the literature also mentions laboratory measurements of anti-inflammatory, anti-elastase and sun-filter activity of extracts [2].
These are properties of extracts in lab assays. Labdanum's strong scent and potential for skin sensitization mean that cosmetic formulations are expected to follow industry usage standards [2].

No studies found. Laboratory research includes a 2020 cell-culture study in which a labdanum fraction suppressed dengue virus replication [5] and reviews of Cistus extracts' antioxidant and antimicrobial properties [4]; these are not human trials.
